steps.action:
# The Last Light of Margery Point

The fog came in the way it always did — not all at once, but in pieces, like a secret being told slowly.

Edmund Foss had kept the light at Margery Point for thirty-one years, and he had learned to read fog the way other men read newspapers. This particular fog was a liar's fog, he decided. It looked thin at the edges but had a thick, grey heart to it that would swallow a ship whole if the light went dark for even twenty minutes.

He climbed the stairs.

He always counted them. One hundred and twelve steps from the base to the lamp room, and he had counted them every single night for thirty-one years, which meant he had counted those steps somewhere in the neighborhood of eleven thousand times, which meant he had, in some sense, climbed to the moon and back without ever leaving this finger of rock that jutted into the North Atlantic like a warning written in stone.

He didn't mind.

People always expected him to mind.

---

His daughter called on the satellite phone every Sunday. She lived in Portland now, taught elementary school, had two boys who called Edmund "Grandpa Lighthouse" because they had visited once, when they were very small, and the beam of light had caught the older one — Thomas — square in the face and made him laugh the way children laugh when something enormous and wonderful happens to them unexpectedly. Edmund kept that memory the way he kept everything important: carefully, in a specific place, where he could find it in the dark.

"Dad," his daughter Clara would say, every Sunday without fail, "you should think about retiring."

"I think about it," he would tell her.

"And?"

"And then I stop thinking about it."

She would sigh. He could hear thirty years of worry packed into that sigh, all the school nights she'd spent in the keeper's cottage doing homework by lamplight while her mother read, all the storms she'd watched from the window, all the times she'd understood, even as a child, that her father's first loyalty was to the sea — or rather, to the people on the sea, which is a different thing entirely.

Edmund didn't think of himself as loyal to the sea. The sea didn't need his loyalty. The sea was indifferent and enormous and had been doing perfectly well before Edmund Foss was born and would continue doing perfectly well long after he was gone. No, his loyalty was to the captains making decisions in poor visibility. To the fishermen heading home. To anyone out there in the dark who needed to know where the rocks were.

That was the job, he always thought. Not keeping the light. Knowing where the rocks are, and making sure everyone else knows too.

---

His wife Margaret had died seven years ago, in November, in a hospital in Rockland, which was forty minutes from the ferry landing, which was twenty minutes from Margery Point, which meant Edmund had been far away in every sense that mattered when it happened.

The light had been on.

He had made sure of that. He had arranged a temporary keeper, a young Coast Guard auxiliary fellow named Brett who was perfectly competent and terrified of the stairs, and Edmund had driven to Rockland and sat with Margaret for four days, holding her hand, watching her breathe in the particular way a person breathes when breathing has become a project rather than a reflex.

On the fifth morning, she had looked at him very clearly — the medication had ebbed and she was herself, entirely herself, in a way that made his throat ache — and she had said, "Edmund, go check on the light."

"I don't need to check on the light."

"I know you don't need to," she said. "I'm asking you to."

He had understood, after a moment, what she was doing. She was giving him permission to be who he was. She had spent forty years doing that, giving him permission to be who he was, and she was doing it one last time, and if he stayed, she would spend her last hours worrying that his presence was somehow a dereliction, that somewhere out in the water a ship was confused because Edmund Foss was sitting in a plastic chair in a hospital room instead of doing what he was made to do.

He kissed her forehead. He drove to the ferry. He checked on the light.

Brett told him everything was fine. Edmund thanked him, shook his hand, stood in the lamp room for a while watching the beam move through the darkness, and when the phone rang two hours later, he answered it already knowing what Clara would say.

He had, on one or two occasions, in the years since, permitted himself to feel guilty about that. But only on one or two occasions, because Margaret would have been annoyed by excessive guilt, and he still had a deep instinct not to annoy Margaret.

---

Tonight the fog pressed against the glass of the lamp room like something alive.

Edmund did his checks methodically. The rotating mechanism was smooth. The lamp was bright and steady, a modern LED array that the Coast Guard had installed five years ago, replacing the original Fresnel lens that now sat in a museum in Bath where tourists could photograph it. Edmund had mixed feelings about the Fresnel lens being in a museum. He understood the practical arguments. He also understood that the lens had been doing its job for a hundred and twenty years before he arrived, and that taking it away felt faintly like ingratitude.

But the LED array was more reliable and used less power and required less maintenance and threw a fine, strong light, so Edmund had made his peace with it.

He stood at the window and looked out at the fog.

Somewhere out there — he was fairly certain, based on the schedule he kept in his head, a habit the Coast Guard found charmingly eccentric — the Penelope Anne was making her way back from the grounds. Captain Jo Sutter, who had been fishing these waters for twenty-five years and knew them as well as anyone alive. She didn't need the light, not really. She had GPS and radar and all the instruments a modern fishing vessel carries.

But she had told him once, over coffee in his kitchen, that she still looked for it. That even with every instrument working perfectly, she still looked for the light at Margery Point and felt better when she saw it.

"Why?" he'd asked.

"Because instruments can fail," she said. "Because electronics have bad nights. Because knowing the light is there means someone is paying attention. Not a satellite, not a computer. A person."

Edmund had thought about that for a long time afterward.

---

At two in the morning, something happened.

It was not dramatic. The most important moments in Edmund's experience rarely were. The mechanism made a sound — small, wrong, a faint grinding at the base of the rotation assembly — and Edmund, who had been dozing in his chair with the particular alertness of a man who has learned to sleep like a cat, was immediately, completely awake.

He went to the assembly and listened and put his hand on the housing and felt the grinding more than heard it. A bearing, he thought. Something in the bearing race.

He opened his maintenance cabinet and found his tools with the ease of long practice, in the dark, without fumbling. He had laid those tools out in the same order for thirty-one years.

The mechanism continued to rotate while he worked — he was careful about that, making sure the light kept moving while he addressed the problem — and after forty minutes of patient, precise work in the tight space around the assembly, he found the culprit: a small piece of grit, almost certainly mineral, that had worked its way into the bearing race and was scoring the metal.

He removed it. He cleaned the race. He re-lubricated the assembly with the particular grease that the manufacturer specified and that Edmund had always found slightly too thin for cold-weather operation, though he'd never been able to convince anyone official of this.

The grinding stopped. The mechanism rotated smoothly. The light continued its patient, sweeping declaration: *here are the rocks, here is the shore, here is where the safe water begins.*

Edmund sat back on his heels and looked at the small piece of grit on his palm. It was nothing. Barely visible. A fleck of the world that had gotten into a place where it didn't belong.

He felt, as he sometimes did after solving a small mechanical problem in the middle of the night, a satisfaction so complete and quiet that it didn't have a name, or rather it had too many names — competence, purpose, belonging, rightness — and so he didn't bother naming it at all. He simply felt it.

He went back to his chair. He looked out at the fog.

Around four in the morning, a light appeared below — the Penelope Anne's running lights, moving steadily through the murk, finding her way in. Edmund watched her pass the point and continue toward harbor, and though she was too far away and the night was too thick for Jo Sutter to see him standing at the glass, he lifted his hand anyway.

The gesture was not for her.

Or maybe it was. He wasn't entirely sure of the distinction.

---

Dawn came sideways, as it does at that latitude in October, slipping under the fog rather than through it, turning the world grey-gold and uncertain.

Edmund made coffee. He sat at his kitchen table with the log open in front of him and wrote his nightly entry in his careful, small hand: visibility, sea state, wind, incidents. He noted the bearing issue and his repair. He noted the Penelope Anne's passage. He noted that the fog was clearing slightly in the east.

He did not note that he had counted the stairs again. He never noted that. It seemed too private somehow, too much his own, to put in an official record.

His coffee grew cold while he sat there, not thinking about anything in particular, just looking at the water, which was beginning to show its true color again as the fog lifted — that specific shade of dark green that belonged only to this water, in this light, at this hour, that he had been looking at for thirty-one years and had never quite been able to describe to anyone's satisfaction, including his own.

Beautiful was the word he always ended up with, which was true but insufficient.

He thought he might call Clara later. Not on Sunday — it was Wednesday — just to call. To ask about Thomas and the other boy, whose name was James but who insisted on being called something Edmund could never quite remember, some name from a video game or a television program that struck Edmund as unnecessarily complicated. He thought he might ask Clara if she remembered the night a storm had knocked out the generator when she was nine and he had kept the lamp burning manually, feeding it by hand, while Margaret sat with Clara and told her stories to keep her calm, and the stories had gone on all night, one after another, until the generator was repaired and the light was steady again.

He thought she probably remembered. It was the kind of thing a person remembers.

He drank his cold coffee and watched the sea and waited for the day to show him what it had.

The light, behind him, kept turning.

---

*That is what it means to keep something*, Edmund thought, though he could not have said exactly when the thought arrived. *Not to own it. Not to control it. Simply to make sure it does not stop.*

He supposed that was true of many things.

He climbed the stairs one more time to do his morning check. He counted as he went.

One hundred and twelve steps.

All present and accounted for.
